# Worksheet: Getting Started

[📥 Download the data (.csv)](data/pine_data.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.csv"} [📥 Download the data (.xlsx)](data/pine_data.xlsx){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.xlsx"}

> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> Work through each part in order, at your own pace. Type every line of code yourself into a **plain R script** — do not copy-paste. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you should type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** ask you to write, modify, or answer something. Boxes marked **🚀 If you finish early** and **Part 15 (Going further)** are optional bonus material.
>
> **Every grey `r` box below is code you type into an R script — not into the Console.** Before you start: **File → New File → R Script**, and save it as `01_getting_started.R` in your project's `scripts/` folder. Then work down the worksheet, adding each block to the bottom of that one script, in order.
>
> **Type the `# ── Part …` header comment at the top of each block, too.** Those comment lines are not decoration — they are how your script stays navigable, how you find your way back to a block that broke, and how I find your work when I read your script. A block with no header comment is a block I cannot place. In RStudio they also show up in the document outline (the `≡` button at the bottom-left of the editor) so you can jump straight to any part.

::: callout-important
## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them
exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length`
will not work:

| Column             | What it is                                     |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file`      | the raw team file the row came from             |
| `team`             | field team — one team = **one tree**            |
| `replicate`        | needle number within a tree side (1-8)          |
| `side`             | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"`           |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres                      |
| `needle_width_mm`  | needle width, millimetres                       |

After you read the file in, run `names(pine_df)` and check the names on your
screen against this table before you write any other code.
:::

# Part 1 · Today's question

### Recap

- We are asking whether pine needle length differs between the **shady** side and the **sunny** side of a tree.
- The **tree**, not the needle, is our unit of replication — one tree is not enough (this is called **pseudoreplication**).

# Part 2 · Build your project folder

### Why a project folder?

Everything for this project lives in **one folder**, so every file path is *relative* to it — no more hunting for where a file went.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §6 — Workflow: scripts and projects](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-scripts.html), and Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 8 (Managing and Curating Data) on Canvas.

### Create the folder structure

Make a new folder called `pine_project`. Inside it, create four sub-folders:

```         
pine_project/
├── data/       ← your CSV and Excel files go here
├── scripts/    ← your .R code goes here
├── figures/    ← plots you save go here
└── output/    ← place to save modified dataframes
```

Copy `pine_data.csv` into `pine_project/data/`.

> ⚠️ **Important:** Leave this copy alone — it is raw data. We will read it but never overwrite it. (Your own field data will get cleaned up and added here starting in Wrangling Your Data.)

# Part 3 · Enter your data in Excel

Before R ever sees your numbers, they have to get from your field notes into a spreadsheet. How you do that now determines how much pain you're in later — so we do it deliberately.

### Set up your header row first

Open Excel and make **row 1** your column headers — nothing else goes in that row. Use the same **controlled vocabulary** your group already agreed on in Part 1, written the `lower_snake_case` way (no spaces, no units hidden in the text): what will they be?

| Column | units? | What goes in it |
|--------|--------|-----------------|
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |
|        |        |                 |

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `Needle Length (mm)` and `needle_length_mm` look equally clear to a human — only one of them is a header R can use without a fight. Spaces, parentheses, and units in the header text all cause problems later.

### One row = one measurement

This is the part people get wrong under time pressure: **every single needle you measured gets its own row.** Not one row per tree with eight length columns crammed in — one row *per needle*, with `team`, `side`, and `replicate` repeated on every row that needle belongs to. Yes, that means typing `shady` over and over. That repetition is doing real work — it's what lets R filter, group, and plot by any of those columns later.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Watch out! — Common Excel data-entry mistakes**

- **Merged cells.** They look nice, they break every import. Never merge.
- **Blank rows or blank columns** used as visual spacers. R reads them as missing data, not as whitespace.
- **More than one header row**, or notes typed above row 1. R will try to read your note as a column name.
- **Numbers stored as text.** `20 mm` in a cell is text; `20` is a number. Keep units in the *header*, not in the cell.
- **Inconsistent spelling of the same category** — `Sunny`, `sunny ` (trailing space), and `sunny` are three different values to R, even though they mean the same thing to you.
- **Color-coding instead of a column.** Highlighting a row yellow to mean something is invisible to R. If it matters, it needs its own column.
:::

### Enter your group's data

**▶ Do this now:** Using the measurements your group collected today, enter one row per needle into Excel using the header row above.

✏️ **Your turn:** How many rows should your sheet have, if your group measured `______________` needles per\
\
side, per tree, on `_____________` trees? Show your arithmetic: `________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Honest preview — this probably isn't "tidy" yet**

Excel *invites* you to spread related numbers across columns — one column per tree, or one column per needle. That's a completely normal way to enter data quickly, and it is **not** the same as *tidy data*: the rule (from *R for Data Science*) that **every variable is a column, every observation is a row, and every value is a cell.** If your sheet doesn't fully follow that yet, that's fine — turning a wide, human-friendly layout into a tidy one is exactly what we'll do with `pivot_longer()` in **Wrangling Your Data**. Today, just get the numbers in accurately.
:::

### Save it — both formats

**File → Save As**, into your `pine_project/data/` folder, **twice**:

1.  Once as an Excel workbook (`.xlsx`) — keeps any formatting you added.
2.  Once as **CSV UTF-8** (`.csv`) — plain text, no hidden formatting, and the format every other tool (including R) can read without a special library.

> ⚠️ **Important:** Save both into `data/`, and — like `pine_data.csv` — treat them as raw data from this point on: read them, never hand-edit them again. Corrections happen in R, where every change is a line of code you can see and undo.

# Part 5 · R as a calculator, and storing values

**▶ Run this in the Console:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · R as a calculator, and storing values ────────────────────
3 + 5
12 / 7
2 ^ 10
sqrt(144)
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** A `+` at the *start* of a console line (instead of the usual `>` prompt) means R is still waiting for you to finish typing something. Press **Esc** to cancel.

Now store a value with the **assignment operator** `<-` (shortcut: Alt/Option + `-`):

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.2 · R as a calculator, and storing values ────────────────────
x <- 7      # store 7 under the name x
x           # read it back
x * 2       # use it in math
```

Look for `x` in the **Environment** pane.

# Part 6 · Naming things well

Good names make code readable months later: be explicit (`needle_length`, not `x2`), never start with a number, and R is **case-sensitive** (`needle_length_mm` ≠ `Needle_Length_mm`). Use `lower_snake_case`.

✏️ **Your turn:** Which of these are valid R object names? Circle Y or N.

```         
needle_length     Y / N
3rd_needle        Y / N
Needle_Length_mm  Y / N
my.needle.data    Y / N
side              Y / N
```

# Part 7 · Comments

Anything after `#` is ignored by R — a note for humans.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · Comments ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# average of four needle lengths, in mm
needle_length <- c(20, 21, 23, 25)

mean(needle_length)   # average needle length
```

> 💡 **Key idea:** If a line confused you while writing it, comment *why* you did it — future you will forget.

# Part 8 · Functions and arguments

A **function** is called by name and takes **arguments** in `()`.

**▶ Run this in the Console:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · Functions and arguments ──────────────────────────────────
sqrt(10)
round(3.14159)             # default: 0 decimal places
round(3.14159, 2)          # 2 decimal places
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)
```

Stuck? `?round` opens the help page.

# Part 9 · Vectors and data types

A **vector** is a series of values built with `c()` which is also called a concatenated list and we will see it more. A spreadsheet column is really just a vector.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 9.1 · Vectors and data types ───────────────────────────────────
needle_length_mm <- c(20, 21, 23, 25)     # numeric vector
side      <- c("n", "s")           # character vector — needs quotes

length(needle_length_mm)   # how many values?
class(needle_length_mm)    # what type?
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `"n"` in quotes is text. Without quotes, R looks for an *object* called `n` and errors if none exists.

# Part 12 · Your first plot

Every `ggplot` is built from three pieces, joined with `+`: **data**, **aes()** (which columns map to x/y), and a **geom** (how to draw it).

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §1 — Data visualization](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize.html). For why we plot before we test, see Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) on Canvas.

**▶ Run this — the simplest possible plot:**

``` r
# ── Part 12.1 · Your first plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_point()
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** The `+` sits at the **end** of a line, never the start.

### Improve it one layer at a time

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 12.2 · Your first plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, color = "tomato") +
  labs(x = "Sun exposure",
       y = "Needle length (mm)",
       title = "Needle length by sun exposure")
```

# Part 13 · Save your plot

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 13.1 · Save your plot ──────────────────────────────────────────
needle_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, color = "tomato") +
  labs(x = "Sun exposure", y = "Needle length (mm)")

ggsave("figures/needle_length.png",
       plot   = needle_plot,
       width  = 3,
       height = 3,
       units  = "in",
       dpi    = 300)
```

Check your `figures/` folder — the PNG should be there.

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `ggsave()` wants the **filename first**, then `plot =`. Always use `dpi = 300`.

# Part 15 · Going further — optional in class, or take-home if you'd like more practice

> Work through this if you finish early. There are no wrong answers — the goal is to see what `ggplot` can do.

### Histograms, split by team

**▶ Try this:**

``` r
# ── Part 15.1 · Going further ───────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, position = position_dodge2(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count", fill = "Sun exposure")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Are the two distributions similar in shape, or different? `________________________`

### Facets — one panel per team

``` r
# ── Part 15.2 · Going further ───────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~team)
```

### Violin plots

``` r
# ── Part 15.3 · Going further ───────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Themes — change the look

Add any of these to a plot above:

``` r
# ── Part 15.4 · Going further ───────────────────────────────────────────
+ theme_bw()
+ theme_minimal()
+ theme_classic()
```

# What your finished project folder looks like

```         
pine_project/
├── data/
│   └── pine_data.csv               <- never touch this
├── scripts/
│   └── 01_getting_started.R           <- your complete script
└── figures/
    └── needle_length.png              <- Part 13
```

This is the structure we will use for **every** analysis this term.

| Folder     | Contents    | Rule                           |
|------------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| `data/`    | raw files   | read-only, never overwrite     |
| `scripts/` | `.R` code   | one script per module          |
| `figures/` | saved plots | always PNG, always `dpi = 300` |

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Spelling? A missing `)` or a `+` at the *start* of a line?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §8 — Workflow: getting help](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-help.html) shows how to write a question others can actually answer.

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
